proseFields.Airbags: Not deployed — interior photos show steering wheel, passenger fascia, and seat bolsters intact with no deployed units visible; no airbag warning evident on the dash display. Confirm A-pillar curtain covers on inspection.
proseFields.Red Flags:
- Cat S on a near-new EV: the visible damage is largely bolt-on, so the structural trigger is most likely intrusion into the chassis leg / inner wing / upper wing support behind the struck corner — a hypothesis to confirm on inspection, not a certainty.
- High-voltage system: any front impact on an EV requires the battery case, HV cable runs, and crash-disconnect status to be verified by an EV-competent technician. Bay photos look clean, but this cannot be cleared from photos.
- Traction battery at 7% charge — not damage, but the car will need charging almost immediately on collection; confirm it accepts charge (charge port flap condition unconfirmed).
- Dash shows wrench/service, brake-system, and TPMS warnings in addition to the park sensor failure — each post-impact fault needs diagnosis (£100–£300 per system if not resolved by the physical repairs).
- Cat S V5 process: the buyer must apply to DVLA for a replacement V5, which will be permanently marked Category S and will show on all HPI checks for the life of the vehicle.
- Parts availability risk: this is a very new model — lead times on OEM body parts and lamps may be long, extending storage/repair time.
proseFields.Bidder Note: Near-delivery-mileage EV with mostly bolt-on visible front damage, but the Cat S marker, unconfirmed suspension/structural extent, and HV verification requirement mean the true repair scope could exceed what the photos show — price the bid for the downside.

proseFields.Confidence Level: Medium — good photo coverage and a confirmed-running, READY-state EV, but the structural extent behind the struck corner, the suspension, and the HV system cannot be cleared remotely.
proseFields.Key Cost Drivers:
1. Two LED headlamp units on a current-generation model — new-model parts with little to no salvage supply yet; OEM pricing dominates.
2. Front suspension/geometry on the damaged corner — the destroyed wheel suggests component damage that could add £500–£1,500+ if arms, hub, or subframe are involved.
3. Cat S structural confirmation — if a chassis leg or inner wing needs pulling/replacement on a jig, add specialist bodyshop time beyond the panel work itemised.
proseFields.Exit Band Position: mid — near-delivery mileage and top trim offset by Cat S structural marker and moderate-to-heavy front corner damage.
proseFields.Margin Calculation: The repair is moderate-to-heavy: predominantly bolt-on front-end components (bumper, beam, wing, lamps, wheel/tyre) per the Parts Breakdown, with the main cost risks sitting outside the itemised lines — suspension components on the damaged corner, possible chassis-leg/jig work behind the Cat S rating, and HV system verification. The exit side is supported by exceptional desirability (a months-old, top-spec EV), but the permanent Cat S V5 marker caps the realistic sale price within the salvage-adjusted band. The margin picture therefore hinges on what the inspection reveals behind the struck corner: if suspension and structure are confined to the visible corner, the itemised repair leaves a workable spread against the code-computed exit value; if chassis-leg or HV damage is confirmed, costs escalate quickly on a new model with OEM-only parts supply. Set the maximum bid to absorb a suspension-and-structure worst case, and remember the hammer price carries Copart fees on top (no VAT on sale on this lot).
proseFields.Recommended Action: Book a £10 Copart WhatsApp video inspection (minimum 48hrs before sale). Significant unknowns — suspension, chassis legs, HV system — are answerable visually. Do not bid blind at strong money on this lot. See checklist below.
proseFields.Realistic Exit Value: Desirability signals are strong: 2026 model year, current-generation car, top "Max" trim with the 54kWh Extended Range battery, 2,681 miles — effectively a delivery-mileage vehicle, which under the newness principle offsets the usual EV caution on battery degradation and resale friction. The live market data (June 2026) frames this: retail £23,030 / £24,472 / £26,023 (low/average/high) and trade £19,576 / £20,801 / £22,119. Against that, the damage is more than light cosmetic — a Cat S marker, a destroyed front corner with probable suspension involvement, and both headlamps implicated — which pulls against the otherwise upper-end desirability. The car runs, drives, and powers to READY with a clean interior, supporting a repairable read rather than a heavy-structural one. Balancing near-delivery desirability against confirmed structural categorisation and a moderate-to-heavy front repair, a mid position within the Cat S band is the coherent call.
proseFields.Visible Damage Summary:
Confirmed body style: 5-door SUV/hatchback (Citroën ë-C3 Aircross, electric). Windscreen sticker suffix: X — insurance company vendor (low value category). The X suffix identifies the vendor type only; write-off status is determined by the Category, confirmed in the listing data as Cat S Repairable Structural.

This is a near-new 2026 EV showing 2,681 miles on the dash photo, which matches the Copart listed mileage exactly — the odometer reading is corroborated.

Primary damage is a substantial front-end strike. The front bumper assembly is completely detached/removed across the full width of the car, exposing the bumper reinforcement beam, the front carrier/slam panel area, and the cooling pack. The reinforcement beam is visible and shows scuffing and impact marks. The damage involves both front corners: on one corner the front wheel is destroyed — the tyre is completely shredded off the rim and the wheel sits abnormally in the arch — with the front wing above it torn and crumpled at its leading edge. On the opposite corner the headlamp unit is visibly unseated and sitting proud of its mounting, with brackets exposed. Headlamp serviceability cannot be confirmed for either lamp: the lamp on the struck corner is not clearly visible in any photo (a loose lamp unit appears to be lying in the engine bay area), and the lamp on the opposite corner, while present, is visibly displaced from its mountings. The bonnet itself appears largely intact, as does the windscreen.

The engine bay photo shows the high-voltage components (inverter, orange HV cabling) in place with no visible deformation or cable damage — but a front impact on an EV always warrants HV system verification, and the green "Electric Vehicle — High Voltage" stickers confirm the yard has flagged it as live HV.

The dashboard photo is valuable: the car powers to READY (consistent with the Run and Drive designation and the "DRIVES" yard annotation), but shows a "Front Park Assist sensor failure" message, a wrench/service warning, TPMS warning, a red brake-system lamp, and a traction battery state of charge of only 7%. The front parking sensors are not visible in their own right (they live in the missing bumper) — the dash message is the evidence of their failure.

Secondary damage: the listing's vendor descriptor "Minor Dents/Scratches" is corroborated by visible scuffing and scratches on one rear quarter panel around the rear lamp, and scuffs on the rear bumper corner. The charge port flap area is shown open with internals exposed — whether the flap/cover is damaged or simply open cannot be confirmed from the photos. The roof, glass, and the opposite flank appear undamaged. Interior is clean and undamaged, consistent with the very low mileage; no airbag deployment visible.

Front suspension on the damaged corner: the destroyed wheel and abnormal sit strongly suggest suspension/geometry involvement, but no specific component damage (arm, hub, subframe) is independently visible — flagged for inspection, see below.
proseFields.Alternative Damage Scenario: The photos are consistent with the listing: a single frontal impact with the bumper assembly stripped (partly by the assessor/recovery, judging by the clean fastener points) and one corner taking the main strike through the wheel. There is no evidence of flood, fire, or theft. The rear quarter scratches are a separate, minor cosmetic event — likely a brush or parking scrape — and should not be forced into the frontal impact narrative.
proseFields.WhatsApp Inspection Checklist:
1. Show the damaged-side front wheel and suspension close up — the wheel is already confirmed destroyed, so direct the handler to the components behind it: lower arm, hub carrier, and subframe mounting, to confirm which have failed.
2. Show the chassis leg and inner wing behind the damaged front corner from below and through the exposed front aperture — looking for deformation, kinks, or creasing that would confirm the structural (Cat S) extent.
3. Show both front headlamps close up — the unseated lamp on the intact corner (lens, tabs, brackets) and whatever remains of the lamp on the struck corner, including the loose unit visible in the engine bay area.
4. Show the orange HV cabling and the underside of the battery case from the front — any visible deformation, scrape, or disturbed connector; confirm the green HV warning state and whether any HV fault shows on the dash.
5. Power the car to READY and ask the handler to engage drive and reverse to confirm it still moves under its own power (keys are present), and read out all dashboard warnings currently displayed.
6. Show the charge port with the flap closed and open — confirm the flap and locking mechanism are intact and undamaged.
7. Show the cooling pack (radiator/condenser) face-on through the exposed front — confirm no fin crush or pipe damage.
8. Inspect the opposite-side front headlamp — on a full-width frontal impact both lamps are implicated; check for displacement, cracking, or moisture ingress and confirm serviceability. Budget ~£350 if replacement needed — flagged as inspection allowance, not included in repair total.
9. Inspect and photograph all four wheels and tyres close-up — confirm no shredding, kerbing, cuts or bulges (the listing photos do not show the wheels clearly enough to confirm condition)
